title: RS256 and ES256: asymmetric tokens
summary: Sign with a private key, verify with the public key, and see why that matters once many services check tokens.

steps.title: The trouble with a shared secret
body: With HS256, the key that **verifies** a token can also **create** one. That's fine for one service. Now picture an identity server and twenty APIs:
- All twenty APIs need the secret to verify tokens.
- So any of them, if compromised (or just careless with logs), can mint tokens for **any user, for every other API**.
- Rotating the secret means changing twenty deployments at once.
**Asymmetric** signatures fix this. You met them in the certificates topic: a **private key** signs, the matching **public key** verifies, and the public key can't be used to sign.
- Only the identity server holds the private key.
- Every API gets the public key, which isn't secret at all. Identity providers publish theirs at a URL (the JWKS, two lessons from now).
- A compromised API can verify tokens but can't forge them.
This is why tokens from Entra ID, Auth0, Okta, Google and Keycloak are signed with **RS256** or **ES256**, not HS256.

steps.prompt: An internal API that only *verifies* tokens is breached and its configuration leaks. With which algorithm can the attacker now mint valid tokens for other services?
options: HS256, because the verification secret is also the signing secret
RS256, because the public key leaked
ES256, because elliptic curves are weaker
steps.explain: With RS256 or ES256 the API only had the public key, which was never secret. The private key stayed on the identity server.

steps.title: The algorithms
body: | `alg` | Signature | Key | Signature size |
| `HS256` | HMAC-SHA256 | shared secret | 32 bytes |
| `RS256` | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256 | RSA, 2048+ bits | 256 bytes for 2048-bit |
| `PS256` | RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 | RSA | 256 bytes |
| `ES256` | ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256 | EC P-256 | 64 bytes |
| `EdDSA` | Ed25519 | Ed25519 | 64 bytes |
RS256 is the most widely supported. ES256 gives much smaller keys and signatures at the same security.
In .NET both are in `System.Security.Cryptography`:
```csharp
using RSA rsa = RSA.Create(2048);
byte[] sig = rsa.SignData(data, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1);
bool ok = rsa.VerifyData(data, sig, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, RSASignaturePadding.Pkcs1);
using ECDsa ec = ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256);
byte[] sig2 = ec.SignData(data, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
bool ok2 = ec.VerifyData(data, sig2, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);

One trap: JWTs carry an ECDSA signature as the raw 64 bytes `r || s` (IEEE P1363), not the DER structure some libraries produce. .NET's `SignData` returns the raw format by default, which is exactly what JWS needs. Java and OpenSSL users often have to convert.

steps.explain: ES256 signatures are 64 bytes (two 32-byte numbers). A 2048-bit RSA signature is 2048 / 8 = 256 bytes. ECDSA signatures also differ every time you sign, because each uses a fresh random number, yet all of them verify.

steps.prompt: Match each `alg` value to its signature scheme.
pairs: HMAC with SHA-256 and a shared secret

steps.prompt: Who should hold each key in a system with one identity server and many APIs?
items: The EC public key, published as a JWK
steps.explain: Public keys are meant to be shared. Only the signer ever needs the private key.

steps.prompt: Verify an ES256 token's signature with the public key.
steps.explain: `VerifyData` hashes the input with SHA-256 for you and checks the 64-byte signature.

steps.title: ES256 by hand
prompt: - `string SignEs256(string payloadJson, ECDsa privateKey)`: header exactly `{"alg":"ES256","typ":"JWT"}`.
- `bool VerifyEs256(string token, ECDsa publicKey)`: three parts, header `alg` is `"ES256"`, and the signature verifies. `false` for anything else, never an exception.

The tests create a P-256 key pair, give `SignEs256` the private key, and give `VerifyEs256` a **separate object holding only the public key**, the way a real API would. They import `System.Security.Cryptography` and `System.Text.Json`.
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
if (!header.RootElement.TryGetProperty("alg", out var alg) || alg.GetString() != "ES256") return false;
catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException)
hints: Same shape as HS256: build the signing input, then `privateKey.SignData(Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(input), HashAlgorithmName.SHA256)`.
Verify with `publicKey.VerifyData(input, FromB64Url(parts[2]), HashAlgorithmName.SHA256)` after checking the header's `alg`.
template: Dojo.Check("the token starts with the ES256 header", dojoTok.StartsWith("eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9."), dojoTok);
Dojo.Eq("the signature part is 86 characters (64 bytes)", 86, dojoTok.Split('.').Last().Length);
Dojo.Eq("the public key verifies it", true, VerifyEs256(dojoTok, dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("another key pair's public key rejects it", false, VerifyEs256(dojoTok, dojoOther));
Dojo.Eq("a tampered payload is rejected", false, VerifyEs256(DojoJwt.Tamper(dojoTok), dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("a token signed by the tests verifies", true, VerifyEs256(DojoJwt.Es("{\"alg\":\"ES256\"}", "{\"sub\":\"grace\"}", dojoPriv), dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("an HS256 header is rejected", false, VerifyEs256(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"sub\":\"ada\"}", new byte[32]), dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("garbage is rejected without throwing", false, VerifyEs256("%%%.%%%.%%%", dojoPub));
public static string Hs(string header, string payload, byte[] secret)
public static string Hs(string payload, byte[] secret) => Hs(Hs256Header, payload, secret);
public static string Es(string header, string payload, System.Security.Cryptography.ECDsa key)

steps.title: RS256 by hand
prompt: Now the same for RSA, the most common algorithm in the wild:
- `string SignRs256(string payloadJson, RSA privateKey)`: header exactly `{"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT"}`, PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, SHA-256.
- `bool VerifyRs256(string token, RSA publicKey)`: as before, with `alg` `"RS256"`.
The tests generate a 2048-bit key and verify with a public-only copy.
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
if (!header.RootElement.TryGetProperty("alg", out var alg) || alg.GetString() != "RS256") return false;
catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException)
template: Dojo.Check("the token starts with the RS256 header", dojoTok.StartsWith("eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9."), dojoTok);
Dojo.Eq("the signature is 256 bytes (342 characters)", 342, dojoTok.Split('.').Last().Length);
Dojo.Eq("RS256 signatures are deterministic", dojoTok, SignRs256("{\"sub\":\"ada\"}", dojoPriv));
Dojo.Eq("the public key verifies it", true, VerifyRs256(dojoTok, dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("a tampered payload is rejected", false, VerifyRs256(DojoJwt.Tamper(dojoTok), dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("an HS256 token is rejected", false, VerifyRs256(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"sub\":\"ada\"}", new byte[32]), dojoPub));
Dojo.Eq("garbage is rejected without throwing", false, VerifyRs256("a.b", dojoPub));
public static string Hs(string header, string payload, byte[] secret)
public static string Hs(string payload, byte[] secret) => Hs(Hs256Header, payload, secret);
public static string Es(string header, string payload, System.Security.Cryptography.ECDsa key)
